Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you turn these notes into a practical draft for warehouse supervisors about a barcode scanning pilot, not a sales pitch and not a finished policy. it should help them understand what is being tried, how work would change, and what questions are still open. keep it grounded in the notes below. we don't have final results, a selected vendor, or an approved budget, so don't write as if any of those exist. this is for a small pilot at the North Dock site, not a plan for every warehouse.

The current problem is that some receiving and picking work is recorded on paper and entered later. That makes it hard to spot a mismatch while the pallet or tote is still nearby. On the other hand, scanning doesn't remove the need to check damaged labels or unclear product descriptions. The draft should explain this balance without claiming that every error will disappear. At North Dock, receiving is on the ground floor and picking and packing cover two aisles plus the packing area. The pilot idea is those two aisles and receiving; don't silently add the rest of the building.

Mara, the receiving lead, says drivers often arrive in a group between 6:30 and 8:00 a.m. The dock has two receiving doors, but door two is sometimes used for returns. A pallet can have a supplier barcode, an internal item label, or both, and the supplier label isn't always readable after wrapping. Luis, a picker, says, “If I find the mismatch at the shelf, I've already carried the tote halfway across the aisle.” He also says that the Wi-Fi signal has been weak near the back end of aisle two, though nobody has measured it recently. Make clear that's a reported concern, not a confirmed coverage test.

Current tools are paper receiving sheets, printed pick lists, and shared handheld scanners. The scanners are Honeywell CT45 units, four currently available for the pilot area, with charging cradles kept by the supervisors' desk. The notes say two scanners have cracked screen protectors; they still work, but the screens are harder to read at an angle. There are no spare batteries recorded. Don't assume more devices or repairs have been arranged. The inventory system is called StockTrack. For now a scan would be expected to look up the item and location in StockTrack; whether it can write changes back immediately is not confirmed. Keep that distinction clear and leave the technical decision open.

The proposed sequence is not settled, but the draft can describe the intended test flow as a proposal: at receiving, scan the pallet or item label, compare the result with the purchase order, and flag a mismatch for a person to check before shelving. At picking, scan the location and item, then confirm the tote before moving on. If a barcode won't scan, staff should be able to use the printed list and write down the problem, rather than stop the whole shift. Don't invent the exact screen messages or say what the system will do after a failed scan. Mention that staff should not scan a damaged or unreadable code repeatedly as a substitute for checking the label.

Dev, the inventory coordinator, wants the first week to include a short start-of-shift check: scanner charge, screen condition, and connection in the work area. He says, “A green light at the desk doesn't tell us what happens at the far end of aisle two.” Use that as an ordinary quote if it fits, and don't turn it into a technical finding. Mara would like a paper fallback kept at both receiving doors. The pilot notes also suggest a quick demonstration before the first shift, but the duration and who will deliver it have not been decided. Don't assign that job to a particular person.

Please include a numbered section with the measures the supervisors could review during the pilot: number of scans that need a retry; mismatches caught before shelving or tote departure; time from delivery arrival to receiving completion; and staff reports of trouble with connection, labels, or screens. These are measures to collect, not goals we've already met. There is no baseline for all four measures, and no target values have been set. Explain that the numbers need context, especially when deliveries arrive together or a label is damaged. Don't promise a percentage improvement or make up a target.

The notes mention a possible two-week pilot, but this is only a suggestion. Any draft should call the length provisional and say that the start date still depends on checking the scanners, confirming what StockTrack can do, and agreeing on the process with receiving and picking staff. No one has decided how many people will participate each shift. There is also an unresolved question about who reviews a mismatch after it is flagged; show it as an open question, not a named responsibility. Don't say the pilot is approved or that the open questions have been answered.

Make the draft easy to use in a supervisor discussion, with a short opening, clear headings, and a closing list of the decisions still needed. Keep the tone practical and cautious. Include the two quotes above exactly if you use them, don't add quotes from other staff, and don't present the notes as customer feedback. Use the terms “receiving,” “picking,” “mismatch,” and “fallback” consistently. Please give the draft a plain title, but don't add an author, date, budget, or company-wide recommendation. ### Current work and site context

Some receiving and picking work is recorded on paper and entered later, making it difficult to notice a mismatch while a pallet or tote is nearby. Explain that scanning may help surface a mismatch earlier, but does not eliminate the need to check damaged labels or unclear product descriptions. Do not claim that all errors will disappear.

Receiving is on the ground floor. Picking and packing cover two aisles and the packing area, but the proposed pilot covers receiving and the two aisles only. The North Dock has two receiving doors; door two is sometimes used for returns. Drivers often arrive in a group between 6:30 and 8:00 a.m., according to receiving lead Mara. Pallets may have a supplier barcode, an internal item label, or both, and wrapping can make a supplier label unreadable.

Picker Luis says, “If I find the mismatch at the shelf, I've already carried the tote halfway across the aisle.” He also reports weak Wi-Fi near the back end of aisle two, though it has not been measured recently. Present this as a reported concern, not a confirmed coverage test.

### Current tools and possible workflow

The current tools are paper receiving sheets, printed pick lists, and shared Honeywell CT45 handheld scanners. Four scanners are currently available for the pilot area. Their charging cradles are by the supervisors' desk. Two scanners have cracked screen protectors; they still work, but their screens are harder to read at an angle. No spare batteries are recorded. Do not assume that additional devices or repairs have been arranged.

The inventory system is StockTrack. A scan is expected to look up the item and location in StockTrack, but it is not confirmed whether the system can write changes back immediately. Keep that technical question open.

Describe the following as a proposed, not settled, test flow:
- At receiving, scan the pallet or item label, compare the result with the purchase order, and flag a mismatch for a person to check before shelving.
- At picking, scan the location and item, then confirm the tote before moving on.
- If a barcode will not scan, staff should be able to use the printed list and record the problem rather than stop the whole shift. Do not invent screen messages or claim to know what the system does after a failed scan. Staff should check a damaged or unreadable label instead of repeatedly scanning it.

### Preparation and fallback

Inventory coordinator Dev suggests a short start-of-shift check during the first week: scanner charge, screen condition, and connection in the work area. Dev says, “A green light at the desk doesn't tell us what happens at the far end of aisle two.” If included, use this quote exactly and do not present it as a technical finding. Mara would like a paper fallback at both receiving doors. The notes suggest a quick demonstration before the first shift, but neither its duration nor its presenter has been decided. Do not assign it to a particular person.

### Measures to review

Include a numbered section listing these possible measures. They are items to collect, not targets already achieved:
1. Number of scans that need a retry.
2. Mismatches caught before shelving or tote departure.
3. Time from delivery arrival to receiving completion.
4. Staff reports of trouble with connection, labels, or screens.

There is no baseline for all four measures, and no target values have been set. Explain that the figures need context, particularly when deliveries arrive together or a label is damaged. Do not invent targets or promise a percentage improvement.

### Provisional timing and decisions still needed

The notes mention a possible two-week pilot, but this is only a suggestion. Call the duration provisional. The start date depends on checking the scanners, confirming what StockTrack can do, and agreeing on the process with receiving and picking staff. The number of participants per shift has not been decided. It is also unresolved who would review a flagged mismatch; show this as an open question rather than assigning responsibility.

Close with a list of the decisions still needed, including the unresolved timing, system capability, process agreement, shift participation, and mismatch review.
